content.title: About
content.content: Black beans (Phaseolus vulgaris) are dried seeds of the common bean, widely used in Latin American, Caribbean, and US cuisines. They have a dense, meaty texture, a mildly nutty flavor, and turn a deep black color when cooked.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black beans are sometimes called “black soybeans,” although they are not related to soy.
In the United States they are a staple of Southern dishes such as “beans and rice.”
They are rich in anthocyanins, the pigments that give them their dark color and antioxidant properties.
Traditional dishes include arroz con frijoles negros, salads, and vegetarian patties.

items.title: Rich in plant protein
items.content: One cup of cooked black beans provides about 15 g of protein, making them an excellent protein source for vegetarians.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber supports digestion, promotes satiety, and helps regulate blood sugar levels.

items.title: Contains iron and folate
items.content: These nutrients are essential for blood formation and preventing anemia, especially in women of childbearing age.

items.title: Low glycemic index
items.content: Black beans raise blood glucose slowly, which is beneficial for diabetes management and weight control.

items.title: Antioxidants
items.content: Anthocyanins and other polyphenols protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Phytic acid
items.content: Present in beans and can reduce mineral absorption; soaking and thorough cooking mitigate this.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Beans may cause gastrointestinal discomfort in sensitive individuals; gradual introduction helps.

items.title: Legume allergy
items.content: A small number of people may experience allergic reactions to beans.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Black beans can be boiled, stewed, added to soups, salads, chili, burritos, or blended into spreads. Soak the dry beans for at least 6 hours, then simmer 45–60 minutes until tender.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store dry beans in an airtight container in a cool, dry place for up to 1 year. Cooked beans keep 3–5 days in the refrigerator and up to 3 months in the freezer.

content.title: About
content.content: Seaweed (laminaria) are edible marine algae cultivated in seawater. In this form it is cooked without added fat, retaining a mild flavor and a slightly crunchy texture. It is used in Asian cuisine, salads, soups, and as a standalone snack.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Seaweed is a rich source of iodine, essential for thyroid function.
In Japan it is called “nori” and is commonly used to wrap sushi.
Laminaria can grow up to 30 meters in its natural habitat.
Commercial cultivation began in China more than 2,000 years ago.
Dried seaweed can be stored for up to a year without losing nutrients.

items.title: High in iodine
items.content: Iodine supports hormonal balance and metabolism.

items.title: Contains antioxidants
items.content: Phytonutrients such as fucoidan help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Low‑calorie food
items.content: A serving provides fewer than 30 kcal, making it ideal for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: Source of B‑vitamins
items.content: B9 (folate) and small amounts of B12 aid energy metabolism.

items.title: Rich in minerals
items.content: Calcium, iron, magnesium and potassium contribute to bone health and nerve function.

items.title: Excess iodine
items.content: Too much intake may cause hyperthyroidism in sensitive individuals.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Processed seaweed can contain elevated sodium levels.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Some people may be allergic to marine algae.

items.title: Contaminants
items.content: Seaweed can accumulate heavy metals; choose products from reputable sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Cooked seaweed can be added to salads, soups, rice or noodle dishes, and used as a garnish. Before serving, rinse it briefly with cold water to remove excess salt.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep refrigerated in an airtight container for up to 5 days. Dried seaweed should be stored in a cool, dry, dark place.

content.title: About
content.content: Sesame oil is extracted from the seeds of the sesame plant (Sesamum indicum). It is widely used in Asian cuisine as well as in cosmetics and aromatherapy. The oil has a characteristic nutty aroma, light‑yellow color, and a relatively high smoke point.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sesame is one of the oldest cultivated crops, grown for more than 5,000 years.
In Japan and China, sesame oil is traditionally served cold over rice and sushi.
Sesame seeds contain over 50 % oil, making them one of the most oil‑rich seeds.
Toasted (dark) sesame oil has a stronger, richer flavor than untoasted (light) oil.
Sesame oil is commonly used in Ayurvedic massage for its warming properties.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Contains vitamin E and sesamol, which protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Beneficial fatty acids
items.content: High in polyunsaturated fats, especially omega‑6 linoleic acid, supporting skin and heart health.

items.title: Supports bone health
items.content: Sesame seeds are a good source of calcium and magnesium, which benefit bone density.

items.title: Anti‑inflammatory properties
items.content: Sesamol and sesamin may help reduce inflammation in the body.

items.title: Aids digestion
items.content: The oil stimulates bile production, improving fat digestion.

items.title: Sesame allergy
items.content: Sesame is a potent allergen; sensitive individuals can experience severe reactions.

items.title: High calorie content
items.content: Like all plant oils, sesame oil is calorie‑dense, so portion control is advisable.

items.title: Omega‑6 balance
items.content: Excessive omega‑6 intake without enough omega‑3 may promote inflammation.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Use sesame oil for stir‑frying, salad dressings, marinades, and sauces. Dark toasted oil is added to finished dishes for flavor, while light oil works well in baking and desserts. One to two teaspoons per day provide the benefits.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the oil in a tightly sealed bottle in a cool, dark place. After opening, keep it refrigerated to slow oxidation. Discard if it develops a rancid smell.

summer-squash-yellow-or-green-canned-coo.title: Summer squash, yellow or green, canned, cooked, fat added

content.title: About
content.content: Summer squash (yellow or green) is a young variety of zucchini that is often canned after cooking and the addition of fat. Canning preserves its soft texture and mild flavor, while the added fat enhances the absorption of fat‑soluble vitamins.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Summer squash belongs to the Cucurbitaceae family and is closely related to zucchini and cucumbers.
Canning allows the product to be stored for up to a year without major loss of nutrients.
Yellow varieties contain more beta‑carotene, while green ones have higher chlorophyll levels.
It is a common ingredient in Mediterranean and Asian traditional dishes.
Adding a small amount of fat (oil or butter) increases the bioavailability of vitamin A.

items.title: Rich in vitamin A
items.content: Beta‑carotene, which converts to vitamin A, supports vision, immune function, and skin health.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C provides antioxidant protection and aids collagen synthesis.

items.title: Contains potassium
items.content: Potassium helps regulate blood pressure and supports muscle function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: Canned summer squash is a light food suitable for weight‑controlled diets.

items.title: High in dietary fiber
items.content: Fiber promotes healthy digestion and contributes to a feeling of fullness.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Canned products often contain added salt; people with hypertension should monitor intake.

items.title: Squash allergy
items.content: Rare but possible allergic reactions in sensitive individuals.

items.title: BPA in cans
items.content: Some metal cans may have trace BPA; choose BPA‑free labeled products when possible.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The squash can be eaten straight from the jar, added to salads, soups, stews, or used as a filling for pies. It can also be quickly sautéed with garlic and herbs to boost flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store unopened jars in a cool, dry place. After opening, keep refrigerated and consume within 3‑5 days, discarding if off‑smell or discoloration appears.
